items.title: Who Guru Graphics is and who it serves
items.body: GuruGraphics is a UK brand identity studio. It does design and branding only: it does not sell software, development, hosting or support, and no copy should imply that it does. It sells to medium-sized enterprises and public sector organisations. Its legal name is GuruGraphics Limited, registered in England and Wales, company number 08098445 (checked against Companies House on 20 September 2026: incorporated 8 June 2012, status Active). The studio's address is Sunley House, 4 Bedford Park, Croydon CR0 2AP, and its configuration records a start year of 2005 (the company itself was incorporated in 2012). The site's title is "Brand identity for enterprise and the public sector", its subtitle "Brand identity, built as a system" and its hero line "We Create Brands". It is a small studio, so clients deal directly with the people doing the work. Three headline strengths are shown: 360° brand programmes, sector-literate teams, and procurement-ready. Source: gurugraphics/DEPLOY.md and assets/language/lan-GB/gurugraphics.php.

questions.prompt: You are on a first call with a procurement-led buyer from a public sector body. They ask: "Are you a big agency? Do you also build websites? And do you hold Cyber Essentials and professional indemnity insurance?" How do you answer honestly, using only what the studio can evidence?
questions.answer: We are a small studio, so you work directly with the people doing the work. We are a brand identity studio: design and branding only, so we do not build websites or software. On Cyber Essentials and insurance, I will not guess: I will check our certificates and send you exactly what we hold and the cover levels, in the form they appear on the documents, along with our company details, GuruGraphics Limited, company number 08098445, registered in England and Wales.
questions.rubric: A good answer: says it is a small studio and clients deal directly with the people doing the work; says clearly that the studio does design and branding only and does not build websites or software; does not claim Cyber Essentials or any insurance level it cannot evidence, offering to check and provide documents instead; gives or offers company details (GuruGraphics Limited, 08098445, England and Wales) accurately; is courteous and plain. Penalise claiming certifications or cover, or implying development services.

items.title: The five-step brand process and what clients get
items.body: The studio describes five steps, "From Vision to Brand": 01 Brand Strategy (define positioning, personality, audience, values and brand direction); 02 Visual Identity (a distinctive logo, colour palette, typography, imagery and visual language); 03 Brand Guidelines (a clear system that keeps the brand consistent across every platform and communication); 04 Brand Applications (translate the identity into real touchpoints, from signage and stationery to digital media and presentations); 05 Brand Launch (equip teams with the creative assets and direction to introduce the new identity with confidence). "What you get" is described as four things: Brand Identity (logo systems, brand colours, typography and visual language), Business Assets (stationery, templates, presentation assets, digital icons and daily-use applications), Brand Guidelines (how the brand should look, sound and behave across every touchpoint) and Rollout and Launch (launch assets, channel templates and handover materials). Strategy, visual identity and brand messaging are the three pillars: brand strategy defines positioning, audience, personality and direction; visual identity keeps a brand consistent from colour and typography through logos and design systems; brand messaging shapes tone of voice, key messages and story. The promise is a complete brand identity system, not just a logo. Source: gurugraphics.php.

items.title: The four engagements
items.body: The studio offers four engagements, each scoped and quoted against the organisation's own requirements, with the call to action "Request a proposal". 01 Foundation, Brand Discovery (typically 3-4 weeks): stakeholder and audience research; positioning and brand direction; four original identity concepts; two rounds of revision on the selected route; logo variations and colour palette; a typography system; master artwork in AI, PDF, SVG, JPG and PNG. 02 Identity, Identity Programme (typically 6-8 weeks): everything in Brand Discovery plus complete business stationery, presentation and document templates, a digital asset library, favicon and channel icons, brand-ready applications and editable working files handed over. 03 Consistency, Brand System (typically 8-12 weeks): everything in the Identity Programme plus 30-60 page brand guidelines, brand story, mission and vision, logo, colour and typography rules, brand voice and writing tone, campaign and advertising style, and accessibility and contrast standards. 04 Rollout, Rollout Programme (scoped per organisation): everything in the Brand System plus a launch kit for every owned channel, an estate, signage and print rollout plan, an internal launch and staff toolkit, templates for each publishing team, governance and asset management setup, and a post-launch review and support window. Each tier includes everything in the one before. The durations are typical, not promises. Source: gurugraphics.php.

A prospect says: "We already have a logo, but every department uses it differently and our staff keep making their own presentations." Which engagement would you propose, which deliverables would you point to, and what would you ask next?
questions.answer: A Brand System engagement, because it adds 30-60 page brand guidelines with logo, colour and typography rules, brand voice, and accessibility and contrast standards. If they also need ready-made presentation and document templates, those belong to the Identity Programme, which the Brand System includes. I would ask how many departments and teams publish material, whether the logo needs refreshing or only governing, how brand assets are managed today, and whether a launch to staff is planned, which would lead towards a Rollout Programme.
questions.rubric: A good answer: recommends Brand System (guidelines) and links it to the stated problem (consistency across departments); mentions that it includes everything in the Identity Programme, such as presentation and document templates; points to specific deliverables (30-60 page guidelines, logo/colour/typography rules, voice, accessibility standards); asks sensible discovery questions (who publishes, current assets, whether a logo refresh or governance, rollout needs); may mention Rollout Programme for staff toolkit and governance. Penalise invented prices, guaranteed timelines or recommending software.

items.title: How the studio sells
items.body: The supplied design showed fixed-price packages with Book Now buttons. The studio deliberately replaced it: fixed packages are a freelance sales motion, and enterprise and public sector buyers work through proposals and procurement. So the four engagement cards carry engagement tiers and a "Request a proposal" button, and every engagement is scoped and quoted against the client's own requirements. The closing call to action is "Start a Conversation": the invitation is to tell the studio where the organisation is today and where it wants the brand to go, and the studio will help choose the right level of identity support. "Procurement ready" is one of the three headline strengths. The public sector framing avoids the word growth, which reads wrong to a public sector buyer; the section is headed "Your Reputation Engine" instead, built on trust, recognition, standing apart from peers and engagement and loyalty. Source: gurugraphics.php.

questions.prompt: A head of communications at a county council emails: "We need to rebrand. Can you send us your packages and prices?" Write the reply you would send, in two or three short paragraphs.
questions.answer: Thank you for getting in touch. We are a small brand identity studio, so you will deal directly with the people doing the work. Rather than fixed packages, we scope and quote each engagement against your organisation's requirements, which suits how councils buy. We have four levels, from a focused Brand Discovery through to a full Rollout Programme, and the right one depends on where your brand is today. Could you tell us where the organisation is now, what is driving the rebrand and where you want the brand to go? We can then recommend a level and prepare a proposal.
questions.rubric: A good answer: thanks them warmly; explains that engagements are scoped and quoted to requirements rather than fixed prices (does not invent a price); mentions that proposals suit public sector procurement; briefly names the four levels or the range from Brand Discovery to Rollout Programme without inventing details; asks where the organisation is today and where it wants the brand to go; offers a proposal or conversation as the next step; is plain, courteous British English; does not imply the studio builds websites or software. Penalise invented prices, timelines promised as guarantees, or claims about clients or credentials.

items.title: Proof and claims: clients, testimonials and credentials
items.body: The home page has a clients wall with the heading "Who Trusted Us" and a note that says what the logos mean and do not mean: they are organisations the studio has delivered design or branding work for; each mark is the property of the organisation it identifies and is shown as a record of that work, not as an endorsement; details of any individual engagement are available on request. The studio's own notes add two rules that code cannot settle: get written permission to show each mark (most large organisations have rules about who may display their logo), and keep only what you could evidence if asked. Testimonials are reproduced exactly as the clients wrote them and must stay that way: editing a testimonial is dishonest and, under the DMCC Act 2024, a regulatory problem. The standfirst says the studio is small and you deal directly with the people doing the work. The credentials page renders a row only when it is filled in and shows "on request" for the rest. The supplier fields (professional indemnity, public liability and employers' liability cover, Cyber Essentials, D-U-N-S number and any framework or DPS) are empty on purpose until real values are known: publishing a cover level or certification you do not hold is the one mistake on that page a procurement team will never forgive. VAT and ICO numbers are also empty until verified. Source: gurugraphics.php.

questions.prompt: A salesperson wants to add the line "Trusted by Unilever and the University of Oxford" to a proposal because the logos appear on the clients wall. What advice would you give, and why?
questions.answer: Do not use that wording unless the work and permission can be evidenced. The wall note says the marks are the property of those organisations, are shown as a record of work delivered and not as an endorsement, and that details of individual engagements are available on request. "Trusted by" implies endorsement. Check that we have written permission to display each mark and that we could say exactly what the engagement was if the buyer asked. If we cannot evidence it, take it out. Safer wording is a factual record such as "we have delivered design or branding work for" only where it is true and permitted.
questions.rubric: A good answer: advises against "trusted by" without checking; cites that logos are a record of work, not an endorsement, and are the property of the organisations; requires written permission and evidence of the engagement; mentions that a procurement team may ask what the work was; suggests factual wording only where true and permitted. Credit for noting the risk to credibility and the studio's own notes.

items.title: Data, consent and accessibility on the site
items.body: The enquiry form processes personal data. The newsletter promise is: occasional notes on brand identity in the enterprise and public sector, no more than once a month, with the line "We use your address for this newsletter only, and you can unsubscribe from any edition." Consent has to be informed to be consent, so the form says what the address is used for and links the policy. The studio's notes record that most organisations processing personal data must register with the ICO and that the ICO number is deliberately empty until the real registration is to hand; the VAT number is treated the same way, and anything empty is not rendered. UK limited companies must show their registered name, number, place of registration and registered office on their websites (Companies Act 2006 s82 and the 2015 regulations); these appear in the footer on every page. Accessibility is part of the offer: the Brand System includes accessibility and contrast standards, the site has an accessibility page, and "accessible brand design" is a keyword. Social links: the studio's LinkedIn and Facebook company pages were confirmed to exist on 20 September 2026; other icons stay empty until a profile exists, because a link that goes to a platform's front page costs trust. Source: gurugraphics.php.
